batch.method: Manual visual correction against rendered PDF pages, using PaddleOCR-VL output only as a scaffold.
policy: Preserve Lovejoy's abbreviations and argumentative structure where readable.
Do not silently normalize difficult ethnographic names, foreign-language titles, or bibliographic references.
Use [illegible]/[?] and confidence flags for uncertain readings.
Where handwriting is too poor for diplomatic transcription, retain only source-supported argumentative structure rather than hallucinating lexical detail.
batch.status: first pass complete; direct-original second-pass argument controls propagated for pp.64-66 and 73

research_signals_from_batch: Lovejoy separates magical/imitative sacrifice from sacrifice directed to personal gods.

PDF p.64 directly describes magical sacrifice as a quasi-technical apparatus whose operator must remain master of it; the manuscript says 'the gods' can exploit a sacrificer's lack of technical skill, correcting the former 'body/power' reading.
Syncretism is treated as a historical process by which originally distinct ritual motives become fused.

PDF p.65 directly says sacrificial forms are not normally found in pure, sharply separated states; two or more are commonly mingled, requiring 'delicate analysis' to dissociate their ritual elements, while fusion/syncretism may have been preceded by a period in which the sacrifices were distinct in character and function.

PDF p.66 adds a performer/jurisdiction distinction: expiatory sacrifice is generally performed by the whole community as it disembarrasses itself of responsibility for a crime, whereas magical sacrifice is performed by priests, specifically those possessing magical skill in charms.
Funerary sacrifice is analyzed as provision and social continuity for the dead before it is read as communion or propitiation.
Human versus animal sacrifice is not accepted as a simple evolutionary index of cultural advancement.
Ritual killing, cannibalism, punishment of specialists, animal sanctity, and sacrifice must be analytically distinguished.

PDF p.73 directly shows explanatory reinterpretation of an inherited funerary practice: a rite initially connected with preventing return of the dead can later be explained through release of the spirit of the corpse/object and transfer of objects to the dead.
Funerary destruction/burning of property can acquire new explanatory rationales over time, illustrating reinterpretation of inherited practices.

pages.corrected_text:
No. 18. Lovejoy describes magical sacrifice as 'a sort of machine' which one should not put into operation unless one is sure of remaining master of it: 'the gods will take advantage of a man's lack of technical skill with the magical apparatus to subject him in turn to their will.' The immediately following characterization of the transaction between god and sacrificer remains partly compressed/uncertain.

But there are also magical sacrifices where one does not even work by way of constraint upon the will of gods, but directly upon the forces of nature. If one wants rain, one makes [an imitative rite], the savage idea being that some strange unity in nature links the act to the desired result.

pages.witness_status: W3 for 'sort of machine', 'the gods', lack of technical skill, and subjection to their will
pages.editorial_argument_summary: The earlier 'body/power' reading is withdrawn. The page models one kind of magical sacrifice as a technically hazardous relation with personal gods, while immediately distinguishing a second kind that acts directly on natural forces.

pages.corrected_text:
[Continuation.] Lovejoy says sacrificial forms are not, in the majority of cases, to be regarded as sharply marked off from one another or as found separately with each idea in its purity. Far more commonly two or more are mingled, so that only by a 'delicate analysis' can one dissociate the different ritual elements. He adds that fusion / syncretism has often been preceded by a period in which the several sacrifices were distinct in character and function; later they become combined.

One common class concerns offerings to the dead. At first naturally food is given to the dead and sacrifice develops from it. The dead receive food, blood, libations of wine, and in some cases human victims. The ideas underlying these offerings are various and often mixed.
pages.transcription_confidence: high for the syncretism/delicate-analysis paragraph; medium for examples
uncertain_readings: A few pronouns/connectives in the first paragraph remain abbreviated.
Some examples of offerings are compressed.
pages.text_layer: direct-image key wording plus conservative summary
pages.witness_status: W3 for mingling, 'delicate analysis', and prior distinctness in character/function
pages.editorial_argument_summary: This is an explicit methodological instruction to decompose a syncretic ritual complex rather than infer one origin from one present form.

pages.corrected_text:
[Funerary sacrifice.] To provide the dead in the future life with what they possessed in life: at a later stage one kills a man/slave so that the dead may have attendants in a condition corresponding to the next life. In the case of royalty or wealthy persons, human beings may be killed at the tomb/table.

On the facing page Lovejoy then distinguishes performance by sacrificial type. In the case of expiatory sacrifice the rite is 'very generally performed' by the whole community; the community thereby disembarrasses itself of responsibility for the crime/offence [middle clause partly compressed]. 'Similarly' / by contrast in organization, magical sacrifice is performed only by priests, and by those priests who possess magical skill in charms. The page therefore connects type of sacrifice with a distinct social bearer or competent ritual agent.

pages.corrected_text: On southern African populations and sacrifice. Distinctions among Bantu, Bushmen, and Hottentot/Khoi groups are noted, with mixtures between them. Lovejoy asks how far sacrificial practices vary with these cultural groupings. In the southern branch, as one moves toward [region uncertain], sacrifice becomes more prominent. Cannibalistic rites and extravagant human sacrifice/massacre in some polities are compared with ordinary funerary killing of wife or slave. The difference may be political/status rather than a fundamentally different religious motive: the king simply has greater power/resources.

pages.corrected_text:
A recent ancestor may retain power and influence after death; offerings/prayers may be addressed to such beings, while magical acts can also be designed to produce an immediate effect without intervention of a personal deity.

Lovejoy cautions against ranking cultures by a simple scale. Funeral sacrifice may be extremely primitive even when elaborate. Animal sacrifice is not necessarily evidence of advancement over human sacrifice; in some contexts the human victim belongs to an older period of extreme respect for a particular dead person. [citation notes follow].
uncertain_readings: citations and some ethnographic wording uncertain

pages.corrected_text: Animal sanctity and sacrifice. References include Cowper Rose, Four Years in Southern Africa. Restrictions on women in relation to cattle/animals are noted. Lovejoy asks whether reverence for animals sacrificed to a deity really implies divinity of the animal. In some cases killing a rain-maker/diviner is punishment for failure to exercise his function effectively, rather than sacrifice to gain rain. Similar cases must be distinguished from genuine religious sacrifice; one cannot infer sacrificial meaning merely from ritualized killing.

[Continuation] One must also distinguish ritual killing from cannibalism. Human flesh may be eaten as a primitive medicine or as a means of driving out/appropriating a spirit, and taboos on eating may have different origins. Such cases provide only cautious evidence for sacrifice proper.
uncertain_readings: opening lines and final examples uncertain

pages.corrected_text:
Funerary sacrifice examples. In S.E. Africa and other regions, men may be killed at the funeral of a chief together with principal wives/attendants. Victims can be chosen from persons having some relation or common life with the deceased. Lovejoy reads this as a form of social/functional continuity: victims are sent to accompany and serve the dead in the other world.

The rite need not involve communion with a god; its immediate purpose is to provide the dead with company, service, or equipment in the future life.
uncertain_readings: specific ethnographic names and citations uncertain

pages.corrected_text: Burning/destruction at funerals is treated as a case of explanatory reinterpretation. Lovejoy first notes a practice connected with protecting the living against the return of the dead, comparing it with placing a heavy stone on a tomb. He then says the practice can develop another meaning, based on the idea that the spirit is not properly released unless the body is completely destroyed; burning becomes the most evident means. On the facing page he compares breaking/smashing objects placed with the dead: destruction can be explained as releasing the soul/spirit of the object so that the dead may have its use in the other world.
pages.transcription_confidence: high for the mechanism of reinterpretation; medium-high overall
uncertain_readings: A few opening/final connective phrases remain compressed.
One clause about the dead person's passage into the other world is not fully diplomatic.
pages.text_layer: direct-image key argument plus conservative summary
pages.witness_status: W3 for original protective rationale, 'another meaning', release-through-destruction, and object-spirit analogy
pages.editorial_argument_summary: The page distinguishes continuity of an outward practice from change in its explanatory rationale; it is direct manuscript evidence for reinterpretation rather than proof of a single original meaning.

pages.corrected_text: References to Cowper Rose, Callaway, Lewis Grout/Zululand and related southern-African material. Sacrificial offerings may superficially resemble totemism or animal worship, but the accompanying rules must be examined before inferring either. Offerings to the dead often have an element of contract or expected advantage, but many are acts of loyalty to a deceased chief rather than payment for a specific favor. Lovejoy stresses that serious offences and propitiatory sacrifice should not be conflated with funerary loyalty.
